chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Khalid Al-Qammat, who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): 'Is the divorce of the fool, the one whose intellect has gone, allowed to be performed by his guardian over him?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Why does he not divorce himself?' I said: 'It is not trusted that if he divorces, he will say tomorrow, "I did not divorce," or he is not proficient in divorcing.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'I do not see his guardian except as being at the status of the Sultan (ruling authority).'

key_terms.الذَّاهِبُ الْعَقْلِ: The one whose intellect has gone/lost
key_terms.الْأَحْمَقُ: The fool/mentally incompetent person (distinct from the insane)

ai.seo_question: What is the legal status of a guardian divorcing a mentally incompetent person in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the guardian (*wali*) of a mentally incompetent man (*al-ahmaq*) acts with the authority of a *Sultan* (ruling sovereign), rather than merely a representative. This elevated status ensures the finality of the divorce, addressing the concern that the incompetent individual might later dispute the act or lack the capacity to execute it properly. This ruling underscores the pragmatic legal necessity of centralized authority in managing the affairs of those lacking full cognitive agency.
